paragraphs.text: Unlike treaties, which bind only the states that ratify them, customary international law is said to bind states generally, arising from a widespread practice that states follow out of a sense of legal obligation. Because custom can thus bind states that never expressly agreed to it, theorists have long sought ways to reconcile it with the principle that sovereign states are subject only to rules they accept. The most celebrated such reconciliation is the persistent objector doctrine, which holds that a state that consistently objects to an emerging customary rule during its formation is not bound by that rule once it crystallizes. Textbooks routinely present the doctrine as settled law and as a vital safety valve for state sovereignty. The doctrine also appeals to intuition: if a state has made its dissent plain from the outset, it seems unfair to hold it to a rule it never accepted merely because others did.
paragraphs.gist: Custom binds generally; the persistent objector doctrine is presented as settled law reconciling custom with consent.

paragraphs.text: Yet the doctrine’s prominence in the literature far outstrips its footing in practice. The authorities most often cited for it are two mid-century decisions of the International Court of Justice, in each of which the Court, having already concluded that the rule in question had not become customary law at all, added that the rule would in any case not apply to a state that had consistently opposed it. Such remarks are dicta: they were unnecessary to the outcome, and a rule that does not exist cannot be applied to anyone, objector or not. Later decisions have occasionally repeated the formula, but almost always in the same posture—as a supplementary observation rather than as the ground of decision. A rule whose every judicial appearance is optional is a fragile foundation for the confidence with which it is taught.
paragraphs.gist: Author: the doctrine rests on thin authority—two ICJ dicta about rules the Court found did not exist.

paragraphs.text: Defenders of the doctrine reply that the scarcity of decisions applying it reflects its success: because states know that objection exempts them, emerging rules are shaped to accommodate likely objectors, so the doctrine rarely needs to be invoked. This reply is ingenious but unpersuasive. The historical record suggests a different pattern. States that resisted the twentieth-century expansion of coastal states’ jurisdiction over adjacent waters, for example, did not secure lasting exemptions; once a large majority of states had embraced the new limits, the objectors conformed. Objection, in practice, has functioned as a bargaining posture during a rule’s formation rather than as a permanent shield after it.
paragraphs.gist: Defenders: scarcity shows success. Author rebuts: objectors historically conformed once majorities formed.

paragraphs.text: None of this means the doctrine is incoherent. It may persist less as an operative rule than as a reassurance—a theoretical device that preserves the image of consent at the foundation of a body of law whose actual development owes more to the gradual convergence of state practice. Scholars would do better to treat the doctrine as a hypothesis about how custom might accommodate dissent than to cite it as an established rule.
paragraphs.gist: The doctrine functions as a reassurance preserving the image of consent; treat it as a hypothesis, not settled law.

paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, legal historians described the medieval lex mercatoria, or law merchant, as a body of customary commercial law that merchants created for themselves. On this account, traders traveling between the fairs and port cities of Europe developed uniform rules of contract, credit, and partnership, which their own courts applied swiftly and independently of kings and municipal authorities. The story has since acquired a second life in economics and political theory, where it is invoked as evidence that commerce can generate and enforce its own law without the state. On this telling, the law merchant was cosmopolitan by nature: a Genoese trader at the fairs of Champagne could expect his contracts to be judged by the same principles as in Bruges or London, because the principles belonged to the merchant community rather than to any prince.
paragraphs.gist: Traditional view: a uniform, merchant-made law merchant, independent of states—now used to argue commerce needs no state.

paragraphs.text: A generation of revisionist historians has subjected this account to sustained criticism. Examining surviving court records, they find that the rules merchants actually litigated over varied considerably from one town to the next, and that the courts hearing merchants’ disputes were usually municipal or royal institutions, not autonomous merchant tribunals. Moreover, when medieval sources refer to ‘the law merchant,’ they frequently mean not a distinct body of substantive rules but a set of procedures—expedited hearings, relaxed rules of proof—suited to litigants who could not wait for the ordinary pace of justice. Merchants, in short, appear in the records less as autonomous lawmakers than as litigants who navigated a patchwork of local jurisdictions, often with the help of local agents and interpreters.
paragraphs.gist: Revisionists: rules varied locally; courts were public; ‘law merchant’ often meant fast procedure.

paragraphs.text: The revisionist case is largely convincing, but it can be pressed too far. Some commercial instruments did achieve remarkable uniformity across jurisdictions. The bill of exchange, by which a merchant in one city could order payment to a creditor in another, came to follow broadly similar conventions throughout much of Europe. That uniformity, however, was produced less by any merchant legislature than by repeated contracting: merchants copied forms that worked, and public courts, faced with those standardized forms, generally enforced them as written. Nor was the process frictionless: courts occasionally refused to enforce terms that offended local rules, and merchants adjusted their forms in response.
paragraphs.gist: Author: revisionists mostly right, but bills of exchange show real uniformity—built by contracting and enforced by public courts.

paragraphs.text: The lesson for modern debates, then, is neither that commerce can dispense with the state nor that its rules must be dictated by one. Private ordering and public authority developed together, each depending on the other. Those who would enlist the law merchant in arguments about the sufficiency of private ordering should recognize that the historical record they invoke tells a more entangled story. Merchants relied on public courts to give their forms teeth, and public authorities, eager to attract trade, learned to accommodate the practices merchants devised.
paragraphs.gist: Private ordering and public authority co-evolved; the history doesn’t support either extreme.

paragraphs.text: The roots of most forest trees are colonized by mycorrhizal fungi, which supply the trees with water and mineral nutrients in exchange for sugars produced by photosynthesis. Because a single fungal individual can colonize the roots of several trees at once, ecologists have proposed that forests are laced with common mycorrhizal networks through which trees exchange resources. In popular accounts, this ‘wood-wide web’ has grown into a striking picture: large ‘mother trees’ are said to nourish their seedlings through the network and to send chemical warnings to neighbors under insect attack. The image has proved irresistible, appearing in bestselling books, documentaries, and even forestry policy debates, where it has been invoked to argue for preserving large old trees as hubs of the network.
paragraphs.gist: Mycorrhizal fungi may link trees in networks; popular accounts claim resource sharing and warnings by ‘mother trees.’

paragraphs.text: That fungal connections between trees exist is not in dispute; researchers have traced individual fungi across the root systems of neighboring trees. More contested is what flows through these connections and to what effect. Experiments in which trees are supplied with carbon labeled by a rare isotope have shown that labeled carbon can later be detected in neighboring trees. Yet such experiments rarely establish the route the carbon took. Carbon released by roots into the soil can be absorbed by neighboring roots or by fungi that are not shared, and most field studies have not ruled out these alternative pathways. Establishing the fungal route would require experiments that block the fungal pathway while leaving soil pathways open, or the reverse—designs that are difficult to implement in intact forests and that few studies have attempted.
paragraphs.gist: Connections exist and carbon moves between trees, but most studies don’t establish the route (soil pathways not excluded).

paragraphs.text: Nor do the quantities involved always support the larger claims. In several studies, the amount of carbon transferred was a small fraction of what the receiving seedlings fixed through their own photosynthesis, too little to account for any meaningful effect on their growth. And claims that trees preferentially direct resources to their own offspring rest largely on greenhouse experiments with seedlings, whose relevance to mature forests is uncertain. A recent review of the field found, moreover, that later papers often cite the earliest positive results while overlooking studies that failed to replicate them, so that the literature conveys more confidence than the underlying evidence warrants. Seedlings grown in pots differ from forest seedlings in light, soil, and the fungal communities available to them, any of which could affect how carbon moves.
paragraphs.gist: Transfers are often small; kin claims rest on greenhouse work; citation bias inflates confidence.

paragraphs.text: None of this shows that the networks are ecologically trivial. It shows that the vivid version of the hypothesis has outpaced its testing. The more productive question is not whether forests are ‘cooperative’ but under what conditions, and by what routes, resources move between plants—a question that only carefully controlled field experiments can answer. Popular accounts have performed a service in drawing attention to the hidden life of soils; the task now is to discipline that attention with evidence.
paragraphs.gist: Networks may matter, but the vivid hypothesis outran evidence; ask about conditions and routes via controlled field experiments.

paragraphs.text: Every translator of verse confronts a choice between fidelity to meaning and fidelity to form. The choice is especially acute with Aleksandr Pushkin’s Eugene Onegin, a novel in verse composed in an intricate fourteen-line stanza of iambic tetrameter with a fixed and demanding rhyme scheme. Most English translators have tried to reproduce the stanza, rhyme and all, accepting that the constraints of English rhyme would force them to bend, pad, or invent meaning in order to land on the required sounds. Each stanza’s rhymes alternate between stressed and unstressed endings in a fixed pattern, and Russian, with its flexible word order and abundance of inflected endings, supplies rhymes far more readily than English does. A translator who insists on the full pattern must therefore spend much of his ingenuity merely meeting it.
paragraphs.gist: Verse translation trades meaning against form; most Onegin translators kept Pushkin’s stanza at the cost of meaning.

paragraphs.text: Vladimir Nabokov’s translation, published in 1964, broke sharply with that practice. Nabokov abandoned rhyme entirely and rendered Pushkin line by line in deliberately literal English, surrounding the text with a commentary several times its length that glosses allusions, traces sources, and records the connotations of individual Russian words. Rhymed versions, he insisted, were not translations at all but imitations that betrayed the original for the sake of a pleasing sound. The commentary was meant to restore what any translation must lose: the echoes of earlier poets, the social codes of Pushkin’s Russia, the weight a particular word carried for a reader of the 1820s.
paragraphs.gist: Nabokov rejected rhyme for literal line-by-line translation plus massive commentary, calling rhymed versions betrayals.

paragraphs.text: The work provoked one of the century’s most celebrated literary quarrels. The critic Edmund Wilson, once Nabokov’s friend, attacked the translation as awkward and pedantic, arguing that it conveyed none of the poem’s grace and that its English was often stranger than the Russian it rendered. Many readers agreed: whatever Nabokov’s version was, it was not a pleasure to read as poetry. Nabokov answered with characteristic scorn, and the exchange, conducted in the pages of literary journals, ended a long friendship.
paragraphs.gist: Wilson and many readers found it awkward and unpoetic.

paragraphs.text: Yet the quarrel rested partly on a confusion of categories. Nabokov’s Onegin is best understood not as a rival to the rhymed versions but as an instrument of a different kind—an apparatus that enables a reader without fluent Russian to approach the original itself, word by word and allusion by allusion. Judged as a substitute for the poem, it fails, as Nabokov himself half conceded; judged as a guide to the poem, it has no equal. The rhymed versions offer an experience of Pushkin’s music at the expense of his sense; Nabokov offers his sense at the expense of his music. A serious reader may need both. To ask which is the true translation is to assume that translation has a single purpose. The question worth asking of any translation is what it enables its reader to do.
paragraphs.gist: Category confusion: Nabokov’s work is a guide, not a substitute; rhymed and literal versions serve different ends.
